answer.answer:
Regulatory exposure in this record shows up in two distinct forms: safety-standard compliance that gates what a robot is allowed to do, and product certification that gates whether a robotically made element can be accepted as building work. Every one of the eight standard-graded dependency links is either a gate onto the same regulatory-compliance node or a risk control that answers it, and all four gating links run to that one node: collaborative work with people, robot design and integration, 3D printed concrete walls and on-site concrete printing each have to clear it before they can proceed. On the deployed side, regulation is recorded as an adoption driver across steelwork, timber and concrete printing processes, including a welding and assembly process from Firm_027 at technology readiness level 9 and a concrete printing process from Firm_115 at technology readiness level 7. What the record does not carry, in the material in front of me, is any Japan-specific statute or approval route, so treat the compliance picture here as the international standards layer rather than the domestic one.

**What compliance actually gates**

The standards layer is small and can be quoted exactly: the graph holds 8 dependency edges graded 'standard', 4 of which gate and 4 of which enable or mitigate, so a standard here is not only a compliance burden. [1] All four gating edges are dependsOn edges onto the same regulatory-compliance node, RI18, and they cover four different problems:

- Working alongside people. Human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards (DEP45: CO6 dependsOn RI18), citing ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025, which replace ISO 10218:2011 and incorporate ISO/TS 15066:2016. [1] The same enabler also has a peer-reviewed dependency on workforce capability: the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce (DEP34: CO6 dependsOn RI6) [1], so the legal problem and the training problem arrive together.
- The machine itself. Robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance (DEP58: AT3 dependsOn RI18) [1], again against ISO 10218.
- Printed structure as a product. 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability (DEP83: PR3 dependsOn RI18), citing ICC-ES AC509 and UL 3401 Ed.2 (2022). [1]
- Getting printing approved on a site. On-site 3D concrete printing proceeds via the IBC Section 104.11 alternative-means approval pathway (DEP84: PR8 dependsOn RI18) [1], that is, by case-by-case evaluation rather than by a prescriptive code clause.

**What answers the exposure**

Two edges are mitigations rather than gates, and both address contact injury (RI20) directly: power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk (DEP57: CO6 mitigates RI20) [1], and speed-and-separation monitoring maintains a minimum protective distance to prevent human-robot contact (DEP91: CO2 mitigates RI20) [1]. The remaining two standard edges are purely enabling: modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components (DEP43: AT7 enablesCapability AR6) [1] and the base module standard reduces component variety and coordinates design, manufacture and assembly (DEP67: AT7 enablesCapability VA7) [1], both citing ISO 2848:1984. Collaborative operation is widely used in the coded record: CO6 is activated in 32 of the 50 coded cases [1]. The activation counts for the regulatory-compliance node and the contact-injury node are not in front of me, so I cannot say how many cases carry them.

**The deployed record**

Regulation is logged as an adoption concern in deployed processes across three materials, and the mix of concerns differs case by case:

- census_RXH5-1, adopted to address regulation, performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core at technology readiness level 9 [2], developed with Firm_027, using steel [3].
- census_RXM4-3, adopted to address regulation, performs 3d printing, assembly and concrete work on the structural core at technology readiness level 7 [4], from Firm_115, and it is the census record of RP15 [3]; RP15 itself is deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, at technology readiness level 7 [5]. This is the deployed case closest to the printing certification and alternative-means problems above.
- census_RXT4-1 pairs regulation with integration and market concerns and performs assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting at technology readiness level 9 [6], from Firm_174, in timber [3].
- census_RXH9-1b combines cost, integration and regulation on the structural core at technology readiness level 9 [7], from Firm_160 [3], and it is the census record of RP5 [3], which is deployed off-site at technology readiness level 9 [8].
- Regulatory concern also appears well below deployment maturity: census_RXM29-4 addresses integration and regulation with material handling at technology readiness level 5 [9], and census_RXM1-1 addresses regulation with inspection at technology readiness level 7 [10].

**Limits worth stating**

None of these case records is linked in the material here to a specific enabler, so I cannot say that any of them activates the compliance node RI18 or the collaborative-operation controls; the regulatory tag on each case and the standards layer are separate pieces of evidence that point the same way. The eight standard-graded edges are a complete set at that grade and may be read as a total, but the co-occurrence list is an explicit cut of the 15 strongest out of 1899 co-occurrence edges [1], and the case set is a retrieval selection widened to robot arms, robotic assembly and mobile vehicles, which is why it leans toward assembly, steelwork and joinery. Absence of a Japanese building-standard clause, a labour-law constraint or a site-permit requirement from this context is not evidence that the wider record lacks one.
